title: Global infrastructure
summary: A Region contains isolated Availability Zones, which each contain multiple data centers. Edge locations form a separate global delivery layer; they are not another Availability Zone.

groups.title: Region · us-east-1
groups.caption: AZs contain data centers; edge locations remain a separate layer.

groups.title: Availability Zone A
groups.caption: Isolated location inside the Region

groups.title: Availability Zone B
groups.caption: Separate AZ failure domain

groups.title: Global edge layer
groups.caption: CloudFront / Route 53 edge locations are outside the AZ hierarchy.

nodes.label: AWS Region
nodes.description: A Region is a geographic area with multiple isolated Availability Zones and a regional service boundary.
nodes.purpose: Choose a Region for latency, service availability, data residency, and recovery requirements.
nodes.example: A workload runs in one Region and uses a second Region only for its recovery plan.

nodes.label: Availability Zone A
nodes.description: An Availability Zone is an isolated location within a Region, composed of one or more data centers.
nodes.purpose: Place redundant zonal resources in separate Availability Zones to reduce correlated failure.
nodes.example: An application load balancer spans two enabled AZs, each with independent application capacity.

nodes.label: Availability Zone B
nodes.description: A second Availability Zone is physically separate from AZ A while remaining in the same Region.
nodes.purpose: Use multiple AZs for regional high availability; this does not by itself provide cross-Region recovery.
nodes.example: A zonal interruption leaves healthy capacity in the other AZ serving requests.

nodes.label: Data center
nodes.description: Data centers contain physical compute, storage, power, and network infrastructure operated by AWS.
nodes.purpose: The customer uses AWS service abstractions rather than selecting an individual data center.
nodes.example: EC2 instances are placed into an AZ, while AWS manages the physical facility.

nodes.label: Data center
nodes.description: An Availability Zone can consist of multiple data centers connected through redundant, high-bandwidth networking.
nodes.purpose: Understand that an AZ is a failure-isolation boundary, not a single building.
nodes.example: Managed services distribute or replicate data across infrastructure according to their documented design.

nodes.label: Data center
nodes.description: Data center facilities inside AZ B are isolated from facilities in AZ A.
nodes.purpose: Separate zonal placement can reduce impact from a localized facility disruption.
nodes.example: A second EC2 target runs in AZ B rather than sharing AZ A placement.

nodes.label: Data center
nodes.description: AWS operates physical facilities and the network connecting them within an Availability Zone.
nodes.purpose: Use service-level AZ placement and health signals rather than attempting to manage a specific building.
nodes.example: An AZ-aware database deployment places standby capacity in a different AZ.

nodes.label: Edge locations
nodes.description: Edge locations are part of AWS global edge infrastructure used by services such as CloudFront and Route 53.
nodes.purpose: An edge location is distinct from a Region AZ and supports latency-sensitive edge delivery or DNS services.
nodes.example: CloudFront caches a static object at an edge location closer to a viewer.

nodes.label: Viewer / DNS client
nodes.description: A viewer connects to a global AWS endpoint, which can direct DNS or content delivery toward an appropriate destination.
nodes.purpose: Distinguish user-facing edge delivery from the regional origin that runs the application.
nodes.example: A viewer resolves a Route 53 record and receives cached CloudFront content when available.

title: IAM authorization flow
summary: Separate the principal that asks to assume a role, the role trust policy, temporary STS credentials, and the policies evaluated for the resource request. An explicit deny overrides an allow.

groups.title: Caller account / identity
groups.caption: Principal and sts:AssumeRole permission

groups.title: Role trust boundary
groups.caption: Role trust policy controls who may assume the role

groups.title: Resource account / policy
groups.caption: Resource policies participate in authorization

nodes.label: IAM user / workload
nodes.description: A user or workload identity is the principal that starts an AWS request. Workloads should normally obtain short-lived credentials through an attached role rather than embedding long-lived keys.
nodes.purpose: Identify who makes the request before reasoning about permissions.
nodes.example: An EC2 application receives role credentials from instance metadata and calls STS or a service API.

nodes.label: IAM group
nodes.description: An IAM group is a collection of IAM users to which identity-based policies can be attached. Groups do not act as principals and cannot be assumed as roles.
nodes.purpose: Use groups to manage shared user permissions, while using roles for delegated or workload access.
nodes.example: An operations group receives read-only console permissions through a group policy.

nodes.label: sts:AssumeRole permission
nodes.description: The caller needs an identity-based allow for sts:AssumeRole on the target role, subject to applicable boundaries and organization controls.
nodes.purpose: This permission authorizes the caller side of role assumption; it does not establish trust by itself.
nodes.example: A build role may assume only the named deployment role in a target account.
services: AWS Identity and Access Management; AWS Security Token Service

nodes.label: IAM role
nodes.description: A role is an identity with permissions that a trusted principal can assume to receive temporary credentials.
nodes.purpose: Use roles to delegate access without distributing long-lived access keys.
nodes.example: A CI identity assumes a narrowly scoped production deployment role for a release.

nodes.label: Role trust policy
nodes.description: The role trust policy is a resource-based policy that identifies principals allowed to assume the role and can constrain the request with conditions.
nodes.purpose: Both caller permission and role trust must permit the intended role assumption.
nodes.example: A trust condition limits assumption to the expected account and federated repository subject.

nodes.label: AWS STS
nodes.description: AWS Security Token Service validates an allowed role-assumption request and returns temporary security credentials.
nodes.purpose: Temporary credentials have a bounded session duration and are preferred for workload access.
nodes.example: An application exchanges its federated identity for a short-lived role session.

nodes.label: Temporary session credentials
nodes.description: An assumed-role session uses temporary access key, secret key, and session token credentials.
nodes.purpose: The credentials carry the assumed role permissions and expire; refresh them through the credential provider.
nodes.example: An SDK default credential chain refreshes the task role credentials automatically.
services: AWS Security Token Service; AWS SDKs

nodes.label: Allow / deny evaluation
nodes.description: AWS evaluates applicable identity and resource policies together with boundaries, session policies, and organization controls as relevant. By default, access is denied and an explicit deny takes precedence.
nodes.purpose: Debug the complete policy context, not just one attached allow statement.
nodes.example: A bucket request fails because an organization policy explicitly denies an otherwise allowed action.

nodes.label: Resource policy
nodes.description: A resource-based policy on a supported resource, such as an S3 bucket, names principals and allowed or denied actions.
nodes.purpose: Cross-account designs often require both caller-side access and resource-owner authorization.
nodes.example: A bucket policy allows one external account role to read a specific prefix.
services: Amazon S3; AWS Identity and Access Management

nodes.label: Protected AWS resource
nodes.description: The service authorizes the signed API call against the request context and applicable policies before granting access.
nodes.purpose: Scope access to the required actions and resource ARNs, then verify any service-specific policy behavior.
nodes.example: The role can read objects under one bucket prefix but cannot change bucket policy.
services: Amazon S3; AWS Identity and Access Management

title: VPC traffic paths across two AZs
summary: The public route table sends internet-bound traffic to the IGW. Private IPv4 egress uses a NAT Gateway in a public subnet in each AZ; ALB requests enter private application subnets through security-group rules.

groups.title: VPC · 10.0.0.0/16
groups.caption: Route tables select targets; SGs attach to resources; NACLs apply at subnet boundaries.

groups.title: Availability Zone A
groups.caption: Public ingress and private app egress path

groups.title: Public subnet A
groups.caption: Route table → IGW · ALB/NAT placement

groups.title: Private subnet A
groups.caption: Route table → NAT A

groups.title: Availability Zone B
groups.caption: Independent targets and AZ-local NAT path

groups.title: Public subnet B
groups.caption: Route table → IGW · ALB/NAT placement

groups.title: Private subnet B
groups.caption: Route table → NAT B

nodes.label: Internet client
nodes.description: A public client starts HTTPS traffic toward the internet-facing load balancer.
nodes.purpose: Public reachability requires a route and public endpoint, plus compatible network rules.
nodes.example: A browser resolves the service DNS name and connects on TCP 443.

nodes.label: Internet Gateway
nodes.description: An Internet Gateway attaches to a VPC and provides a route target for internet traffic; it is not itself a firewall.
nodes.purpose: A public subnet needs a route to the IGW, and public IPv4 instances need a public address for direct internet access.
nodes.example: The public ALB receives inbound traffic through the IGW.

nodes.label: Public route table
nodes.description: The public subnet route table includes the VPC local route and an internet default route to the IGW.
nodes.purpose: The route table determines next hops; it does not grant traffic through security controls.
nodes.example: 0.0.0.0/0 points to the attached IGW for the public load balancer and NAT gateways.

nodes.label: Private route table A
nodes.description: Private subnet A has a local VPC route and a default IPv4 route to the AZ-local NAT Gateway for outbound internet initiation.
nodes.purpose: Using an AZ-local NAT path avoids routing private traffic through a NAT Gateway in another AZ.
nodes.example: Application patch downloads leave through NAT A and return through the established connection.

nodes.label: Internet-facing ALB
nodes.description: The ALB is deployed in public subnets across enabled AZs and forwards requests to healthy targets.
nodes.purpose: Use the ALB security group to allow client listener traffic and application-target traffic separately.
nodes.example: The ALB forwards HTTPS requests to app targets on the configured target port.

nodes.label: NAT Gateway A
nodes.description: A public NAT Gateway allows private IPv4 resources to initiate outbound connections while preventing unsolicited inbound initiation.
nodes.purpose: A NAT Gateway must be placed in a public subnet whose route reaches the IGW.
nodes.example: A private app instance reaches an external package repository through NAT A.

nodes.label: Private app target A
nodes.description: An application target in the private subnet has no direct public ingress route; the ALB security group is permitted to reach its listener.
nodes.purpose: Keep application targets private and scope their security-group ingress to the ALB security group.
nodes.example: The ALB forwards a request to an EC2 target in AZ A.

nodes.label: Public route table B
nodes.description: The AZ B public subnet route table sends internet-bound traffic to the IGW.
nodes.purpose: Public route associations are per subnet and must be deliberately configured.
nodes.example: NAT Gateway B uses this table to reach the IGW.

nodes.label: Private route table B
nodes.description: Private subnet B routes internet-bound IPv4 traffic through its own AZ-local NAT Gateway.
nodes.purpose: Provide independent egress paths per AZ when cross-AZ dependency is not desired.
nodes.example: Private application traffic in AZ B uses NAT B.

nodes.label: NAT Gateway B
nodes.description: A second NAT Gateway supplies an egress path for private resources in AZ B.
nodes.purpose: A single NAT Gateway can create an AZ dependency and cross-AZ transfer; plan availability and cost together.
nodes.example: App B sends outbound requests through NAT B in the same AZ.

nodes.label: Private app target B
nodes.description: An application target in AZ B provides capacity independent from the AZ A target.
nodes.purpose: Spread targets across AZs and configure health checks so unhealthy targets stop receiving requests.
nodes.example: The ALB routes a request to the healthy target in AZ B when AZ A target is unhealthy.

nodes.label: Subnet NACL + resource SGs
nodes.description: Network ACLs are stateless subnet controls with allow and deny rules; security groups are stateful allow-only controls attached to resources.
nodes.purpose: Route tables decide paths; NACLs and security groups filter packets at different boundaries.
nodes.example: Permit ALB-to-app traffic in SG rules and ensure NACL return ephemeral ports are allowed.
services: Amazon VPC; Security Groups; Network ACLs

title: EC2 Auto Scaling behind an ALB
summary: DNS resolves clients to the ALB. The ALB forwards to healthy target-group instances; CloudWatch metrics inform Auto Scaling policies that change desired fleet capacity across AZs.

groups.title: AWS Region
groups.caption: Regional load balancer and Auto Scaling group

groups.title: Availability Zone A
groups.caption: ALB subnet + private EC2 target subnet

groups.title: Public subnet A
groups.caption: Regional ALB enabled in this AZ

groups.title: Private EC2 subnet A
groups.caption: No direct public ingress

groups.title: Availability Zone B
groups.caption: Independent ALB subnet + EC2 target subnet

groups.title: Public subnet B
groups.caption: Regional ALB enabled in this AZ

groups.title: Private EC2 subnet B
groups.caption: No direct public ingress

nodes.label: Route 53 alias
nodes.description: Route 53 resolves the application name to the regional load balancer.
nodes.purpose: DNS directs clients to the ALB; it does not distribute each HTTP request between EC2 instances.
nodes.example: An alias record targets the application load balancer.

nodes.label: Application Load Balancer
nodes.description: An ALB accepts HTTP(S) traffic and routes it to a target group based on listener rules.
nodes.purpose: Spread the ALB over public subnets in multiple AZs.
nodes.example: Listener rule forwards /api requests to the service target group.

nodes.label: EC2 target group
nodes.description: The target group registers EC2 instances and evaluates configured health checks.
nodes.purpose: Only healthy registered targets should receive traffic.
nodes.example: A failing health check removes an instance from request routing while Auto Scaling replaces capacity.

nodes.label: Auto Scaling group
nodes.description: The ASG maintains desired EC2 capacity across selected subnets and replaces instances that fail configured health checks.
nodes.purpose: Use a launch template and multi-AZ subnet placement to manage fleet capacity.
nodes.example: The group launches a replacement instance after an unhealthy instance is terminated.

nodes.label: EC2 instance · AZ A
nodes.description: An EC2 instance runs the application and registers as a target in the target group.
nodes.purpose: Instances should be stateless or use external state so replacement and scaling are safe.
nodes.example: A launch template provisions a new web instance in AZ A.

nodes.label: EC2 instance · AZ B
nodes.description: A second EC2 instance in another AZ provides independent serving capacity.
nodes.purpose: Use multiple AZs and test behavior when one target or AZ becomes unhealthy.
nodes.example: The target group serves traffic from AZ B during an AZ A issue.

nodes.label: CloudWatch metrics
nodes.description: CloudWatch metrics report workload and fleet signals that can be used by scaling policies.
nodes.purpose: Choose a metric that reflects demand or saturation and set evaluation periods carefully.
nodes.example: ALB request count per target drives a target-tracking scaling policy.

nodes.label: Scaling policy
nodes.description: A scaling policy adjusts desired capacity according to metrics or scheduled actions.
nodes.purpose: Scaling changes desired count; it does not itself guarantee fast application startup or enough subnet IPs.
nodes.example: A target-tracking policy increases desired capacity as requests per target rise.
services: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling; Amazon CloudWatch

title: S3 access, protection, and replication
summary: S3 requests are authorized through IAM and bucket policy evaluation. Object versioning, encryption, and lifecycle are bucket/object controls; optional Cross-Region Replication asynchronously copies eligible object versions to a versioned destination.

groups.title: Source Region · S3 bucket
groups.caption: Objects, versions, encryption, and lifecycle policy

groups.title: Destination Region
groups.caption: Separate bucket and independent destination controls

nodes.label: Application client
nodes.description: A client makes an authenticated S3 API request over TLS.
nodes.purpose: Use a role or federated identity and avoid exposing long-lived access keys.
nodes.example: A service requests GetObject for a permitted object key.
services: Amazon S3; AWS Identity and Access Management

nodes.label: IAM identity policy
nodes.description: The caller identity policy grants only the required S3 actions and resource scope.
nodes.purpose: Identity-based allow is one part of the authorization decision; explicit denies and resource policies still matter.
nodes.example: A workload role permits reads for one bucket prefix.
services: AWS Identity and Access Management; Amazon S3

nodes.label: Bucket policy
nodes.description: The bucket policy controls resource-based access, including public-access blocks and allowed principals.
nodes.purpose: Keep block-public-access enabled unless a carefully reviewed public use case requires otherwise.
nodes.example: A bucket policy allows the application role and denies insecure transport.

nodes.label: S3 bucket
nodes.description: An S3 bucket is a regional object namespace whose objects are stored by S3 across multiple AZs.
nodes.purpose: S3 is object storage; use bucket and access settings to define protection and sharing.
nodes.example: An application stores generated reports in a private bucket.

nodes.label: Objects / versions
nodes.description: Objects contain data and metadata; with versioning enabled, overwrites and deletes retain version history.
nodes.purpose: Versioning supports recovery from accidental changes but does not replace independent backup or retention controls.
nodes.example: A prior object version is restored after an accidental overwrite.

nodes.label: Encryption · SSE-KMS
nodes.description: S3 encrypts objects at rest; SSE-KMS uses a KMS key and requires both S3 and KMS authorization as applicable.
nodes.purpose: Protect key access and verify key policy, IAM permissions, and service use.
nodes.example: The application role can read objects only when it has permission to decrypt with the selected key.
services: Amazon S3; AWS Key Management Service

nodes.label: Lifecycle policy
nodes.description: Lifecycle rules transition or expire objects and noncurrent versions according to configured age and filters.
nodes.purpose: Match lifecycle behavior to access patterns, retention obligations, and restore requirements.
nodes.example: Older logs transition after the active investigation window and expire only after retention ends.

nodes.label: Cross-Region replication
nodes.description: S3 replication asynchronously copies eligible object versions to a destination bucket in another Region when configured with versioning and permissions.
nodes.purpose: Replication supports geographic separation but is not synchronous and does not automatically mirror every configuration.
nodes.example: A compliance archive copies new object versions to a separate Region.

nodes.label: Destination bucket
nodes.description: A destination bucket stores replicated object copies under its own policy, encryption, and retention configuration.
nodes.purpose: Test destination access and recovery independently from source-account access.
nodes.example: Recovery operators retrieve replicated objects after a regional incident.

title: Route 53 DNS failover
summary: A client resolver receives an answer from the hosted zone routing policy. Health status informs the primary/secondary DNS answer; clients must still reconnect and honor DNS caching behavior.

groups.title: Region A · primary
groups.caption: Primary ALB and health evaluation

groups.title: Region B · secondary
groups.caption: Failover ALB must be ready for traffic

nodes.label: Client
nodes.description: The client asks its recursive resolver for the service DNS name.
nodes.purpose: DNS routing chooses an answer; the client then connects to the returned endpoint.
nodes.example: A browser resolves api.example.com before starting HTTPS.

nodes.label: Recursive resolver
nodes.description: The resolver queries the authoritative hosted zone and caches the answer according to DNS TTL.
nodes.purpose: Keep TTL and failover expectations in mind; DNS changes are not instant connection migration.
nodes.example: A client resolver asks Route 53 for the alias record.

nodes.label: Public hosted zone
nodes.description: The hosted zone stores authoritative records for a domain.
nodes.purpose: Use alias records for supported AWS targets and select a routing policy deliberately.
nodes.example: An A/AAAA alias points to the primary regional ALB.

nodes.label: Failover routing policy
nodes.description: A Route 53 failover policy associates primary and secondary records and returns the secondary when health evaluation marks the primary unhealthy.
nodes.purpose: Health evaluation and DNS TTL affect failover behavior; test the complete client recovery path.
nodes.example: Primary alias is returned while its configured health signal is healthy.

nodes.label: Health checks
nodes.description: A Route 53 health check can monitor a configured endpoint or other supported signal; alias records can also evaluate target health.
nodes.purpose: Choose endpoint checks or Evaluate Target Health according to the architecture; do not assume the health check understands application semantics.
nodes.example: A health check detects the primary endpoint is not responding and marks its record unhealthy.

nodes.label: Primary ALB · Region A
nodes.description: The primary regional ALB serves the production endpoint while targets are healthy.
nodes.purpose: Place the ALB across multiple AZs and ensure its target health represents service readiness.
nodes.example: Traffic goes to the primary ALB under normal conditions.

nodes.label: Secondary ALB · Region B
nodes.description: A secondary regional endpoint is the failover destination and must have recoverable data and deployable application capacity.
nodes.purpose: DNS failover alone does not provision capacity, synchronize state, or guarantee application readiness.
nodes.example: A warm standby ALB receives DNS answers after the primary is deemed unhealthy.

title: Lambda event processing and failure handling
summary: The diagram shows asynchronous invocation: Lambda queues the event and applies the async retry policy. The execution role authorizes downstream API calls; exhausted or expired events can go to a configured DLQ or on-failure destination.

groups.title: AWS Region · async invocation
groups.caption: Event source, function, execution role, and destinations

nodes.label: EventBridge / S3 event
nodes.description: An event source invokes Lambda synchronously or asynchronously according to the integration. This diagram shows an asynchronous invocation path.
nodes.purpose: Know the invoker retry model; event-source mappings such as SQS have different source queue retry and redrive behavior.
nodes.example: An EventBridge rule sends a matching event to the function asynchronously.
services: Amazon EventBridge; Amazon S3; AWS Lambda

nodes.label: Lambda async queue
nodes.description: For asynchronous invocation, Lambda queues the event before attempting function execution.
nodes.purpose: The event may be delivered more than once; make handlers idempotent.
nodes.example: A queued event waits until function concurrency is available.

nodes.label: Lambda function
nodes.description: Lambda runs the function in a managed execution environment and scales concurrency within configured limits.
nodes.purpose: Keep function code safe for retries and manage timeout, memory, concurrency, and downstream limits.
nodes.example: The function validates a document event and writes normalized metadata.

nodes.label: Execution role
nodes.description: The execution role grants the Lambda runtime permission to access required services and write logs.
nodes.purpose: The role is assumed by Lambda; it is distinct from a caller permission to invoke the function.
nodes.example: A function role can write one DynamoDB table and its CloudWatch log group.
services: AWS Identity and Access Management; AWS Lambda

nodes.label: DynamoDB / S3
nodes.description: Downstream service APIs are called using credentials from the execution role.
nodes.purpose: Grant only the actions and resource ARNs needed by the function.
nodes.example: A document processor writes metadata to DynamoDB and output to S3.

nodes.label: Retry policy
nodes.description: Lambda asynchronous invocation retries function errors according to its configured retry and event-age settings.
nodes.purpose: The default retry behavior applies to asynchronous function errors; synchronous caller and event-source mapping retries differ.
nodes.example: A transient downstream error causes a bounded retry; duplicate handling avoids duplicate writes.

nodes.label: On-failure destination / DLQ
nodes.description: A configured dead-letter queue or on-failure destination captures events that fail processing or expire, depending on configuration.
nodes.purpose: Monitor destination delivery failures and define a controlled redrive process.
nodes.example: SQS stores an exhausted event for investigation and later replay.

nodes.label: CloudWatch logs / metrics
nodes.description: Lambda emits logs and metrics to CloudWatch when execution role permissions and logging configuration allow it.
nodes.purpose: Monitor errors, throttles, duration, concurrency, and async event age.
nodes.example: An alarm detects rising function errors and queue age.

title: ECS, ECR, and Fargate delivery path
summary: Source is built and scanned, then an immutable image is stored in ECR. ECS schedules Fargate tasks in private subnets across two AZs; the execution role supports platform image/log actions, while the task role supplies application permissions.

groups.title: VPC · workload account
groups.caption: ALB in public subnets; Fargate tasks in private subnets

groups.title: Public subnets
groups.caption: Internet-facing ALB only

groups.title: Availability Zone A
groups.caption: Task ENI in private subnet

groups.title: Private subnet A
groups.caption: No direct inbound internet route

groups.title: Availability Zone B
groups.caption: Task ENI in private subnet

groups.title: Private subnet B
groups.caption: No direct inbound internet route

nodes.label: Source repository
nodes.description: The source repository contains application code and the Docker build definition.
nodes.purpose: A protected pipeline builds a versioned artifact from reviewed source.
nodes.example: A commit starts CI and creates a traceable image digest.

nodes.label: Docker build + scan
nodes.description: A build job produces a container image, runs tests and security checks, then tags the immutable digest.
nodes.purpose: Build once and promote the same digest; avoid embedding secrets in image layers.
nodes.example: CodeBuild tests the image before pushing it to ECR.

nodes.label: Amazon ECR
nodes.description: ECR stores container images and provides the registry endpoint used by ECS tasks.
nodes.purpose: Configure repository policies and image retention appropriate to rollback needs.
nodes.example: The task pulls the exact image digest from the private repository.

nodes.label: ECS service
nodes.description: The ECS service maintains desired task count and deployment state for its task definition.
nodes.purpose: ECS service scheduling coordinates task placement; networking and IAM roles are configured in the task definition/service.
nodes.example: A new task definition revision rolls out across private subnets.

nodes.label: Application Load Balancer
nodes.description: The ALB receives public HTTPS traffic and forwards requests to healthy ECS task targets.
nodes.purpose: Place it in public subnets and restrict task ingress to its security group.
nodes.example: An ALB target group routes to task ENI addresses on the application port.

nodes.label: Fargate task · AZ A
nodes.description: A Fargate task runs in a private subnet with its own task network interface and security groups.
nodes.purpose: Use private subnets and provide required egress through NAT or VPC endpoints.
nodes.example: The task receives ALB traffic through the target group and calls a backend service.

nodes.label: Fargate task · AZ B
nodes.description: A second Fargate task provides capacity in another AZ.
nodes.purpose: Multi-AZ placement improves availability but requires sufficient subnet IPs and healthy task placement.
nodes.example: ECS replaces a stopped task in AZ B while the AZ A task continues serving.

nodes.label: Task execution role
nodes.description: The execution role is used by the ECS agent or Fargate platform for actions such as pulling private ECR images and publishing logs.
nodes.purpose: It does not provide application code credentials inside the container.
nodes.example: The platform uses this role during image pull and log setup.
services: Amazon ECS; AWS Identity and Access Management

nodes.label: Task role
nodes.description: The task role provides temporary credentials to application code inside the container.
nodes.purpose: Grant only application API permissions; keep it separate from the task execution role.
nodes.example: The service code reads a specific DynamoDB table using its task role.
services: Amazon ECS; AWS Identity and Access Management

nodes.label: VPC endpoints / egress
nodes.description: Private tasks reach AWS services through VPC endpoints or an intentionally configured egress path.
nodes.purpose: A private subnet has no direct IGW route; endpoint policies and security groups still govern access.
nodes.example: ECR image and CloudWatch log traffic uses configured VPC endpoints rather than public internet routing.

title: CloudWatch signals to response
summary: Resources publish metrics and logs to CloudWatch. Metric alarms evaluate time-series thresholds and can notify responders through SNS; logs and dashboards support diagnosis rather than serving as the alarm condition in this flow.

groups.title: AWS Region
groups.caption: Regional metrics, logs, alarms, and notification services

nodes.label: AWS resources
nodes.description: Applications and AWS services emit metrics, logs, and service events.
nodes.purpose: Instrument application signals as well as infrastructure metrics so alerts map to user impact.
nodes.example: An ALB emits request and target health metrics while the application writes structured logs.
services: Amazon EC2; Elastic Load Balancing; AWS Lambda

nodes.label: CloudWatch metrics
nodes.description: Metrics are timestamped values grouped by namespace and dimensions.
nodes.purpose: Choose dimensions that support useful aggregation without uncontrolled cardinality.
nodes.example: Request count and 5xx rates are emitted for service and target group dimensions.

nodes.label: CloudWatch Logs
nodes.description: CloudWatch Logs stores log events in log groups and streams with configured retention and access.
nodes.purpose: Use structured logs and protect sensitive data; set retention intentionally.
nodes.example: The Lambda execution role sends application output to its log group.

nodes.label: CloudWatch alarm
nodes.description: An alarm evaluates a metric over configured periods and enters states such as OK, ALARM, or INSUFFICIENT_DATA.
nodes.purpose: Use meaningful evaluation periods and missing-data handling to reduce noisy or blind alerts.
nodes.example: An ALB 5xx rate alarm enters ALARM after the chosen datapoints breach the threshold.

nodes.label: Dashboard / Logs Insights
nodes.description: Dashboards and Logs Insights help operators correlate metric trends with log events.
nodes.purpose: Dashboards aid investigation but do not replace paging alarms or service-level objectives.
nodes.example: An operator uses a dashboard time window to inspect logs around an alarm.

nodes.label: SNS notification
nodes.description: An alarm action can publish a notification to an SNS topic with configured subscribers.
nodes.purpose: Control who receives notifications and ensure the action path is tested.
nodes.example: An alarm publishes to an operations topic that fans out to email or an incident integration.

nodes.label: On-call responder
nodes.description: The responder receives an alert and follows a runbook to determine impact and mitigation.
nodes.purpose: Include enough context, ownership, and links to reduce time to diagnosis.
nodes.example: The responder correlates alarm time with deployment history and logs.

title: CI/CD from commit to verified release
summary: A pipeline builds and tests a source revision, scans and stores an immutable artifact, deploys it, then checks service health. A CloudWatch alarm can stop or roll back a traffic-shifting deployment when configured.

groups.title: Delivery pipeline
groups.caption: Build, validation, artifact promotion, and deployment stages

groups.title: Production account
groups.caption: Deployed service and health-gated rollback

nodes.label: Git repository
nodes.description: A reviewed source change starts the release workflow.
nodes.purpose: Protect release branches and identify the source revision for every artifact.
nodes.example: A merge to the protected branch triggers a pipeline execution.

nodes.label: CI/CD pipeline
nodes.description: The pipeline coordinates source, build, test, approval, artifact, and deployment stages.
nodes.purpose: Use least-privilege role sessions and separate production controls from build permissions.
nodes.example: CodePipeline passes a successful build artifact to the deploy stage.

nodes.label: Build + tests
nodes.description: The build stage compiles, tests, scans dependencies and images, and emits a versioned artifact.
nodes.purpose: Fail before promotion when tests or security policies fail; preserve artifact provenance.
nodes.example: CodeBuild creates and scans one container image digest.

nodes.label: ECR / artifact store
nodes.description: The registry or artifact store holds immutable outputs that are promoted across environments.
nodes.purpose: Promote the tested artifact instead of rebuilding different bytes for production.
nodes.example: The pipeline records and deploys an ECR image digest.

nodes.label: Deployment stage
nodes.description: A deployment controller applies a task definition or release to the target environment.
nodes.purpose: Choose rolling or traffic-shifting deployment according to capacity and rollback constraints.
nodes.example: CodeDeploy shifts traffic to a new ECS task set after health checks pass.

nodes.label: Production service
nodes.description: The service runs the deployed version behind a load balancer and emits health signals.
nodes.purpose: Use target health and application metrics to validate user-facing readiness.
nodes.example: The new ECS service revision receives a canary share of traffic.

nodes.label: CloudWatch alarms
nodes.description: Alarms evaluate release health signals such as error rate and latency during rollout.
nodes.purpose: Select actionable thresholds and avoid relying on a single infrastructure metric.
nodes.example: A sustained 5xx increase stops the traffic shift.

nodes.label: Rollback / prior revision
nodes.description: A configured deployment strategy can stop or roll back a failed rollout to a known prior revision.
nodes.purpose: Rollback is not a substitute for backward-compatible database changes or retained artifacts.
nodes.example: A failed canary routes traffic back to the prior healthy task set.

title: Multi-AZ availability and cross-Region recovery
summary: Multi-AZ resources reduce zonal disruption impact inside Region A. Cross-Region replication or copied backups address regional recovery with different RPO and consistency properties; Route 53 shifts new connections only after the DR environment is ready.

groups.title: Region A · primary
groups.caption: Multi-AZ application + database availability

groups.title: Availability Zone A
groups.caption: Primary workload placement

groups.title: Availability Zone B
groups.caption: Standby / distributed application placement

groups.title: Region B · recovery
groups.caption: Warm standby, replica, and copied recovery points

groups.title: Recovery Availability Zone
groups.caption: Recovery capacity and data destination

nodes.label: Clients
nodes.description: Clients resolve a service name and connect to the currently active regional endpoint.
nodes.purpose: DNS failover requires a ready destination and reconnecting clients.
nodes.example: Route 53 shifts new DNS answers to the DR ALB after health evaluation.

nodes.label: Route 53 failover
nodes.description: A failover routing policy returns the primary record while healthy and the secondary record when primary health fails.
nodes.purpose: DNS is only one part of failover; validate TTL, health evaluation, data readiness, and client retry behavior.
nodes.example: The secondary ALB receives new connections after a regional failure.

nodes.label: Primary regional ALB
nodes.description: The primary regional ALB is enabled in public subnets across the primary Region AZs and forwards to healthy application targets.
nodes.purpose: DNS returns this endpoint while its configured health evaluation is healthy.
nodes.example: The ALB forwards connections to the active application tier in either healthy AZ.

nodes.label: Primary RDS
nodes.description: The primary database serves writes in Region A. Multi-AZ standby replication is for availability inside the Region and is distinct from cross-Region DR.
nodes.purpose: Use database-native or service-supported cross-Region replication when a regional recovery point is required.
nodes.example: A regional DB outage promotes the Multi-AZ standby; a regional outage requires the DR plan.

nodes.label: Multi-AZ standby
nodes.description: A Multi-AZ standby improves database availability within the primary Region; it is not a cross-Region read replica in the standard deployment model.
nodes.purpose: Do not treat Multi-AZ failover as protection against loss of the entire Region.
nodes.example: RDS performs a managed failover to the standby in another AZ.

nodes.label: AWS Backup vault
nodes.description: AWS Backup recovery points preserve configured resources according to backup plan and vault retention.
nodes.purpose: Protect backup administration and test restores; a recovery point is not proof of successful application recovery.
nodes.example: A scheduled backup is copied to a separately controlled DR Region vault.

nodes.label: Primary app · AZ A
nodes.description: An application target runs in the primary Region AZ A and serves requests behind the regional ALB.
nodes.purpose: Keep application state external so another AZ or Region can serve after recovery.
nodes.example: An EC2 or ECS target in AZ A serves while AZ B capacity remains healthy.

nodes.label: Primary app · AZ B
nodes.description: A second application target runs in AZ B behind the same regional load balancer.
nodes.purpose: Multi-AZ application placement reduces the impact of a single AZ failure.
nodes.example: The ALB routes traffic to the AZ B target during an AZ A impairment.

nodes.label: Cross-Region data copy
nodes.description: Supported data replication copies state to the DR Region with service-specific consistency and lag characteristics.
nodes.purpose: Replication is not necessarily synchronous and can replicate logical deletion or corruption.
nodes.example: S3 Cross-Region Replication asynchronously copies eligible objects; database replication uses its own semantics.

nodes.label: Warm standby app
nodes.description: The DR Region contains application capacity that can be brought to service during recovery.
nodes.purpose: Choose pilot-light or warm-standby capacity based on RTO, cost, quotas, and tested automation.
nodes.example: The deployment pipeline can scale the standby service after regional failover.

nodes.label: DR database / replica
nodes.description: A cross-Region replica or restored database provides DR data according to the chosen replication or backup mechanism.
nodes.purpose: Validate replication lag, promotion procedure, consistency, and application connection changes.
nodes.example: Promote the supported replica or restore a recovery point before redirecting writes.

nodes.label: Recovery regional ALB
nodes.description: The recovery Region has an ALB endpoint ready to receive traffic when Route 53 fails over.
nodes.purpose: A failover record points to a real, healthy endpoint; DNS does not create or scale this resource.
nodes.example: The DR ALB starts serving after standby capacity and data are ready.

nodes.label: Recovery objectives
nodes.description: RTO is the target time to restore service; RPO is the target maximum data-loss window.
nodes.purpose: Choose architecture and test scenarios against measurable objectives, not labels alone.
nodes.example: A business defines an RPO and RTO, then measures restore and failover exercises.

title: Three-tier application across two AZs
summary: Route 53 resolves to CloudFront, where AWS WAF can inspect viewer requests. Dynamic origin traffic reaches a public ALB, then private application targets, then an isolated private database tier with a separate security-group boundary and Multi-AZ database standby.

groups.title: AWS Region
groups.caption: Regional application VPC and database deployment

groups.title: VPC · tiered subnets
groups.caption: Routes and security groups enforce tier boundaries

groups.title: Availability Zone A
groups.caption: Independent application and database placement

groups.title: Public subnet A
groups.caption: Regional ALB network interface placement

groups.title: Private application subnet A
groups.caption: App SG accepts traffic from ALB SG

groups.title: Private isolated DB subnet A
groups.caption: Database listener allowed only from app SG

groups.title: Availability Zone B
groups.caption: Second AZ for app and database failover

groups.title: Public subnet B
groups.caption: Regional ALB network interface placement

groups.title: Private application subnet B
groups.caption: App SG accepts traffic from ALB SG

groups.title: Private isolated DB subnet B
groups.caption: Database standby remains nonpublic

nodes.label: Internet client
nodes.description: Clients resolve the public application name and establish TLS to the edge or load-balancing endpoint.
nodes.purpose: Use DNS and edge caching to route users; protect origins from direct bypass where appropriate.
nodes.example: A user opens www.example.com and receives a CloudFront distribution address.

nodes.label: Route 53
nodes.description: Route 53 resolves the application hostname to the CloudFront distribution.
nodes.purpose: DNS provides name resolution and routing policy, not HTTP request inspection.
nodes.example: An alias record points the site hostname to CloudFront.

nodes.label: CloudFront + AWS WAF
nodes.description: CloudFront delivers content from edge locations; AWS WAF web ACL can be associated with CloudFront to inspect and filter requests.
nodes.purpose: CloudFront is appropriate for edge caching and global delivery; WAF placement and scope must match the protected resource.
nodes.example: WAF blocks a malicious request before it reaches the origin; cacheable static content is served at the edge.

nodes.label: Regional ALB
nodes.description: The ALB is the application origin in public subnets and forwards permitted requests only to the application tier.
nodes.purpose: Restrict origin ingress to the intended CloudFront origin path where configured, and allow app ingress only from the ALB SG.
nodes.example: A dynamic API request reaches the ALB and is routed to a healthy app target.

nodes.label: App tier · AZ A
nodes.description: Application instances or tasks run in a private subnet and accept traffic from the ALB security group.
nodes.purpose: Keep app targets private and avoid direct client ingress.
nodes.example: The app tier validates a request and opens a database connection.
services: Amazon EC2; Amazon ECS; Amazon VPC

nodes.label: App tier · AZ B
nodes.description: A second private application subnet in another AZ provides independent capacity.
nodes.purpose: Configure load balancing and scaling so one AZ can carry the required failover load.
nodes.example: ALB health checks stop routing to an impaired AZ target.
services: Amazon EC2; Amazon ECS; Amazon VPC

nodes.label: Database security group
nodes.description: The database security group allows only the database listener from the app-tier security group.
nodes.purpose: Security groups are stateful; use references between tier security groups rather than broad CIDRs.
nodes.example: The database accepts TCP 5432 only from application instances in the app SG.

nodes.label: Private RDS primary
nodes.description: The database resides in isolated private subnets and is not publicly accessible.
nodes.purpose: Use Multi-AZ for availability where appropriate; the standby is for failover and is not ordinarily a read endpoint for standard RDS Multi-AZ.
nodes.example: Application connections use the writer endpoint; Multi-AZ failover changes the underlying primary.

nodes.label: RDS standby · AZ B
nodes.description: A standby in another AZ supports managed Multi-AZ failover for supported RDS configurations.
nodes.purpose: A standby is not a substitute for backups or cross-Region recovery.
nodes.example: RDS fails over to the standby during a supported AZ interruption.

nodes.label: Trust boundaries
nodes.description: Each tier has its own route placement and security-group boundary: edge/origin, ALB/app, and app/database.
nodes.purpose: A private subnet alone does not define access; combine routing with stateful security-group rules and carefully managed NACLs.
nodes.example: Inbound database traffic is permitted from the app SG only; the DB subnet has no IGW route.
